title: Help everywhere
hook: Guru Gobind Singh, be our help everywhere

segments.voice: Yesterday: nau nidh, the nine treasures, and your line: nine treasures home. Today, the tenth Guru, and the last line of the opening stanza.

Here's a detail that's easy to miss when the Ardas goes by at full speed. Guru Gobind Singh wrote its opening stanza. He names Guru Nanak, then each Guru after him, one by one, all the way to his own father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. And then he stops. Of course he doesn't name himself: it's his poem. But Sikhs who pray the Ardas today hear the tenth Guru's name right after the ninth, in exactly the same words. Someone added it, and the words they chose had been sitting at the end of the stanza all along.
screen: `THE TENTH GURU WROTE THE STANZA.` → `HE STOPS AT HIS FATHER.` → `SOMEONE ADDED HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: The stanza ends: sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, be our help in every place. Sabh is all. Thaaeen is places. Sahaai, an old friend by now, is the helper. So the Var's opening asks every Guru it has named to be our help, everywhere. Then the Ardas, as Sikhs pray it, goes on: dasvaan paatshaah, sri guru gobind singh sahib ji, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai. The tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, be our help in every place. The community took the poem's last line and gave it to the poet. The one who left himself out is written back in. And it fits him. He became Guru as a boy, after his father's execution. He wrote poetry and, tradition says, kept a court of poets at Anandpur. He founded the Khalsa. He fought battles, lost his sons, and lived through siege, flight and grief. And before his death, Sikh tradition says, he ended the line of human Gurus: from then on the Guru would be the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa community. So this isn't a vague wish. It's asked of someone remembered in the court and on the battlefield, in the forest and in grief. Sikhs ask him to be present wherever they go: the job interview, the hospital waiting room, the long drive home. And the prayer doesn't ask for help in some places. Sabh thaaeen. All of them.
screen: `SABH THAAEEN: IN EVERY PLACE.` · `THE POEM'S LINE, GIVEN TO THE POET.` · `A LIFE THAT WENT EVERYWHERE.` · `ALL PLACES, NOT SOME.` · then, large: `HELP EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Think of the places you'll be this week, your desk, your car, a hard conversation, your own kitchen late at night, and pick the one where you feel most alone. Picture yourself there. If you pray, ask in the Ardas's own words, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, and feel that it includes this place; if you don't, picture someone you trust standing beside you.
Help everywhere. Sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai: the last line of the tenth Guru's stanza, which the Ardas gives back to him.
Your line: present in every place. That includes the one you pictured. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 619 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LIGHT OF THE TEN.`

original.note: Gurmukhi: sabh thaaeen, in every place; the refrain that closes the Ardas's opening stanza.

trapdoor: what you thought: help everywhere is a general blessing.
what it means: it's the stanza's last line, given back to the tenth Guru, asking for help in every single place.
what a scholar hears: the Var's first pauri ends sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai after Guru Tegh Bahadur; the line naming Guru Gobind Singh is a later addition by the Panth.

chat.says: The Ardas asks Guru Gobind Singh to 'be our help in every place.' Where's that line from?
options: His own stanza ended with it; the community gave the line back to him, the poet who left himself out.
He wrote it about himself, naming his own help last as the greatest of all the Gurus.
It's a later hymn about battle, asking for his help only on the battlefield.
chat.meaning: Guru Gobind Singh's stanza stops at his father. The Ardas adds his name using the stanza's own last line, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai.

Anandpur.meaning: the town where, tradition says, the tenth Guru kept poets

Khalsa.meaning: the community of initiated Sikhs Guru Gobind Singh founded

Guru Granth Sahib.meaning: the Sikh scripture, honored as the living Guru
